top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) answers a first-order question about who gains and loses when technology and trade shift labour demand. It pairs a skill-demand framework with transparent local-labour-market designs, and a decade or more of replication and critique has refined magnitudes and persistence without overturning the qualitative findings. The citation should be worded around labour demand, wages and regional employment, not the task model as theory, which limits overlap with the Acemoglu, Goldin and Card prizes. The costs are real: Dorn is excluded under the three-name cap, the technology and trade strands could be read as two achievements, and China-shock magnitudes remain contested. If the committee narrows the scope to import competition, Autor-Dorn-Hanson would be the right set. I still prefer P001 because it credits both strands the citation names. P002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) has the cleanest attribution and is mature, but it is mainly theoretical, its quantitative importance is identified more indirectly, and it needs a stated separation from the 2022 prize. It is a defensible second choice. No award is last, since both proposals describe substantive, mature achievements.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile for the credited names in P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) or P002 (Kiyotaki, Moore). My listed co-authors are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I disclose institutional ties to committee colleagues (SSE affiliation with Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Stromberg; Lund colleague Enflo). My market-design background may bias me toward applied, cross-disciplinary work. Noted, not adjudicated.
